subject: biology-1
question: At low substrate concentration, doubling the substrate doubles the rate of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction. When substrate is present in great excess, doubling it again barely changes the rate. What best explains this plateau?

options.text: The excess substrate destroys the enzyme, so fewer active sites remain.
The activation energy rises when substrate becomes more abundant.
The product builds up and inhibits the reaction through feedback inhibition.
The enzyme molecules are already saturated, so all active sites are occupied and extra substrate cannot speed things up.

explanation: At high substrate concentration all active sites are occupied, so the rate is limited by the number of enzyme molecules and adding more substrate has no effect. Excess substrate does not destroy the enzyme (A), and the activation energy does not rise with substrate abundance (B). Product accumulation can inhibit an enzyme (C), but it does not explain the plateau in the initial rate at saturation.
